Palestinian doctor Hussam Abu Safiya held without charge in Israel for two years

Channel 4 News releases a report on Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, a paediatrician and former medical director of Kamal Adwan hospital in northern Gaza, who was abducted by Israel and held without charge since December 2024.
 
A year and a half later, he is at imminent risk of being killed in Israel’s notorious Nitzan Prison, after being held captive for more than 550 days.
 
His lawyer said that in his most recent meeting last Thursday, Dr Abu Safiya showed signs of severe beating around the head, struggled for breath and to talk and was in fear of his life.
 
Last week the advocacy group Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) warned that his life is in imminent danger and demanded his immediate release.
 
On Wednesday, PHRI said the Israeli state had rejected a high court petition for Abu Safiya and other doctors to be released.

Thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday in the Iranian holy city of Qom during a fourth day of marathon funeral proceedings for the late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Aerial footage broadcast by state television showed the streets of Qom - home to about 1.5 million people - packed with mourners.

An estimated millions have gathered on the streets of Tehran to participate in the funeral procession of former supreme leader Ali Khamenei.

'Everything just kept detonating' — Devastating Russian attack hits quiet Kyiv suburb of Vyshneve

Residents of the small town of Vyshneve, on Kyiv's western edge, have described scenes of terror amid Russia's latest devastating missile and drone attack on the capital, as they found themselves fleeing a series of massive explosions after a strike on the town.

"A huge mushroom cloud rose into the sky. Burning fragments kept flying behind us. They were so high, but it felt like everything was on fire," Diana Liashchuk, 21, told the Kyiv Independent.

"I called my mom just to tell her not to worry, that I was alive. Then another huge explosion happened. I was terrified she would hear me die over the phone."

📰 Police arrested 14 activists in central London on Sunday after they staged a protest marking one year since Palestine Action was banned, inviting officers to join the proscribed group.

Standing outside New Scotland Yard, the headquarters of the Metropolitan Police, activists from Defend Our Juries handed out leaflets urging serving officers to join Palestine Action.

Police arrested the demonstrators under Section 12 of the Terrorism Act, which criminalises inviting support for a proscribed organisation and carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison.

The arrests mark an escalation in the policing of the campaign.

The peace in Ukraine that worries NATO

A potential ceasefire would provide Ukraine a much-needed respite — but would raise difficult security questions for NATO states along Russia’s frontier. European defense planners are increasingly sounding the alarm about the prospect of battle-hardened, modernized Russian armies freed for deployment along the Baltic or Nordic borders.

How far Russia is willing and able to push will depend not only on the alliance’s ability to respond firmly, but also on the eventual shape of any armistice in Ukraine.

Iranians take to the streets to mourn supreme leader Khamenei ahead of his funeral

“For many people like me, one of the ways to relieve the stress is to be present in the rallies.”

On Thursday, Iranians gathered on the streets of Tehran to mourn the death of supreme leader Ali Khamenei ahead of his funeral. People sang and chanted among pictures of their late leader.

Khamenei was killed in joint US and Israeli air strikes on 28 February, the first day of the war on Iran. He had been the leader of Iran since 1989, when his predecessor Ruhollah Khomeini died.

Khamenei’s funeral will begin on Saturday and continue until Thursday, when he will eventually be buried in his home city Mashhad.

Dr Nika Soon-Shiong said she was removed from the board of the Committee to Protect Journalists after challenging a decision she feared would see Palestinians broadly excluded from journalist death tolls. She told MEE “there are bad faith attacks” on the organisation seeking to lobby against Palestinians’ inclusion.

Last week, the CPJ said it was reviewing its documentation of journalists killed during the Israel-Gaza War. 20 Palestinians were delisted after militant groups published obituaries identifying them as members. But Soon-Shiong's fears surround sweeping changes to how the CPJ redefines "journalist". International law protects the civilian status of journalists working for state or militant groups on the condition they are not directly involved in combat.

The CPJ’s board has since voted to reaffirm their original definition in a move welcomed by Soon-Shiong.

An Israeli bill to restrict the adhan, the Muslim call to prayer, passed a preliminary reading in parliament on Wednesday.

Palestinians condemned the legislation as a "declaration of religious war" and an attack on freedom of worship.

The bill passed by 50 votes to 36 and must now be referred to a Knesset committee before returning for its first reading. It would then need to pass second and third readings before becoming law.

The legislation was introduced by Zvika Fogel, a lawmaker from National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir's party.

Under the proposal, mosques would be prohibited from installing or operating loudspeaker systems without a permit.

Permits would be granted according to criteria set by the Israeli authorities, including noise levels, sound-reduction measures, a mosque's location, its proximity to residential areas and its impact on nearby residents

In this op-ed, Dr Amina Shareef, a researcher of anti-Muslim racism, explains how the Palestine Action court battle casts a spotlight on the flawed assumptions linking terrorism to the racialised image of the Muslim threat.

Iran was knocked out of the World Cup on Saturday but their government is painting it as a victory. Whether or not it’s the moral victory they depict, unprecedented levels of international support for the ousted team points to a plausible PR victory in the wider context of the war.

Iran’s football fate was sealed by two last-minute plot twists, earning them the BBC title of "unluckiest side in World Cup history". But global commentators hit back hard: not “luck”, they said, but “sabotage”, “discrimination” “corruption” – by the hosting USA.

Was Iran the unluckiest team in World Cup History– or the worst treated? And while the Iranian team lost the battle on the pitch, did they score a bigger victory on the geopolitical playing field?

On today's MEE Live, Mathilda Mallinson was joined by MEE journalist Rayhan Uddin to weigh up the narratives of injustice against Iran.

Investigation: How EU machinery keeps feeding Russian missile makers

Russian metallurgical plants that supply the country’s defense industry during Russia’s war against Ukraine have imported EU-made equipment despite the restrictions aimed at preventing it.

An intermediary, set up in Turkey and owned by a Dutch national, helped supply the banned machinery to Russia, according to customs records obtained by the Kyiv Independent and IrpiMedia.

The records show that the Turkey-based company Redwing Metal shipped $5 million worth of equipment in 2023 and 2024 to two plants in Russia: Aluminum Metallurg Rus (AMR) and Stupino Metallurgical Company (SMK).

Intercepting the Ukrainian An-196 Liutyi kamikaze drone presents greater challenges compared to intercepting the Iranian "Geran" (Shahed) drone. The An-196 Liutyi has a cruising speed of approximately 120–160 km/h, whereas the "Geran" cruises at around 185 km/h. The minimum radial speed for engaged targets by many air defense systems typically ranges from 100–180 km/h. Depending on the target's flight path relative to the air defense system, the radial velocity can be significantly lower than the target's actual airspeed. Consequently, a slow-flying drone such as the Liutyi may be more difficult to detect, track, or engage under certain conditions.
